title: What Gets You Moving
objective: After this level you can explain drives, homeostasis and incentives as sources of motivation.
summary: Motivation is what steers behavior toward a goal. Drives push from inside when the body slips out of balance, and incentives pull from the world outside.

cards.headline: Nobody pays you to drink when you're thirsty. Yet a paycheck works too.
cards.body: So what actually gets you moving? Psychologists define motivation as the wants or needs that direct behavior toward a goal. Their answers split in two: one force pushes from inside your body, and another pulls from out in the world.

cards.headline: Your body keeps a balance
cards.body: The first answer starts inside you. Your body works to hold things at a steady level, a balance called homeostasis. When it slips, say your blood sugar drops, you get a drive, hunger, that pushes you to eat until balance returns. Drive theory adds a twist: whatever ended the drive last time, you're likelier to do again. A snack that worked at 4 p.m. yesterday has a head start today.

cards.headline: Pulled, not pushed
cards.body: Drives can't explain everything. Incentive theory says rewards and goals out in the world pull you toward them, while drives push from within, and most behavior mixes both. Even a lab animal shows the difference. In a Skinner box, an animal normally presses a bar for water when it's short of water. Under special conditions, it presses for water it doesn't need. No drive is pushing; the reward alone is pulling.

mascot.line: Common mix-up: drives push from inside your body; incentives pull from outside. Most of what you do has a bit of both.

items.label: Drive (push)
points: Starts with a need inside the body
Low blood sugar brings hunger; eating restores balance

items.label: Incentive (pull)
points: Starts with a reward or goal in the world
Pulls you toward it, alongside any drive

cards.headline: Motivation: mapped
learned: Motivation directs behavior toward a goal
Drives push when the body slips out of balance
What ends a drive tends to become a habit
Incentives pull from the world outside

questions.prompt: Match each idea with what the cards say about it.

pairs.right: Hold things at a steady level
Starts with a need inside the body
A reward or goal in the world

questions.explanation: Homeostasis is your body's work to hold things at a steady level. A drive pushes, starting with a need inside the body. An incentive pulls, starting with a reward or goal in the world.

questions.prompt: According to drive theory, why does a drop in blood sugar lead you to eat?

options.label: Food is always the most rewarding thing around
options.rationale: That would be an incentive story, not drive theory.

options.label: It breaks the balance and creates a hunger drive
Eating is a habit that ignores the body
options.rationale: In drive theory, the habit grows from reducing the drive.

options.label: Low blood sugar makes food taste better
options.rationale: The card explains a need and a drive, not taste.

questions.explanation: A drop in blood sugar breaks homeostasis, creating a need felt as hunger, which pushes you to eat until balance returns.

questions.prompt: Level 5's Skinner used rewards to change animals' behavior. In incentive theory, what does such a reward do?

options.label: It pushes from inside, like thirst
options.rationale: Pushing from inside is what drives do.

options.label: It restores the body to balance
options.rationale: That is what satisfying a drive does.

options.label: It stops the behavior from repeating
options.rationale: Rewards were used to strengthen behavior, not stop it.

options.label: It pulls behavior toward it from outside

questions.explanation: Incentives pull behavior toward them from the outside world; a Skinner-box animal will even press a bar for water it doesn't need.
